Whitening strips.summary: Peroxide-coated films that lighten tooth discoloration; the American Dental Association has accepted some of them, and peroxide bleaching is well documented.
Whitening strips.overview:
Whitening strips are thin, flexible plastic films coated with a peroxide gel, typically hydrogen peroxide at roughly 6 to 14 percent, that are pressed onto the front teeth for a set time each day over one to several weeks. They are sold over the counter and are the most widely used consumer route to lighter teeth.

In appearance terms they target extrinsic and mild intrinsic discoloration from coffee, tea, wine and age, and are generally regarded as one of the lower-cost and better-supported cosmetic options for the smile. Results fade gradually, and many users repeat short touch-up courses.
Whitening strips.mechanism: Hydrogen peroxide diffuses through enamel and breaks down into reactive oxygen species that cleave the large pigmented molecules lodged in the tooth, converting them into smaller, less colored fragments. The strip holds the gel against the tooth surface so the peroxide stays in contact long enough to act.
Whitening strips.risks: The main side effects are transient tooth sensitivity and gum irritation, usually mild and resolving after stopping. Strips cover mostly the front teeth and fit unevenly on crowded or irregular teeth, so coverage can be patchy. The Cochrane review of home bleaching rated much of the evidence as low certainty, while reporting that peroxide whitening itself is consistently shown to lighten teeth. Dental guidance generally advises seeking dental advice before overuse, or before whitening over untreated decay or exposed roots.

Whitening gel trays.summary: Trays holding peroxide gel against all tooth surfaces; coverage is more even than strips, and dentist-fitted trays are a standard option.
Whitening gel trays.overview:
Whitening gel trays are soft plastic trays loaded with a carbamide or hydrogen peroxide gel and worn over the teeth for minutes to hours at a time. They come as custom-fitted trays made by a dentist from impressions or scans, or as boil-and-bite and prefilled over-the-counter versions.

Because the tray holds gel against every tooth surface, coverage is more even than with strips, and dentist-supervised take-home bleaching is regarded as a standard cosmetic dental option.
Whitening gel trays.mechanism: Carbamide peroxide breaks down into hydrogen peroxide and urea, and the released peroxide oxidizes pigment molecules inside enamel and dentin. A well-fitted tray keeps gel in constant contact with the teeth and away from the gums, allowing longer, lower-concentration exposure.
Whitening gel trays.risks: Tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are the common effects and are typically temporary; poorly fitting trays let gel leak onto the gums. A meta-analysis found tray carbamide peroxide and hydrogen peroxide systems comparable overall, and supervised trays give slightly larger measured color change than strips, though the difference may not be visible. Ill-fitting low-cost trays lose much of the coverage advantage, and a dental check beforehand is commonly recommended.

LED whitening kit.summary: Peroxide gel combined with a blue or violet LED mouthpiece; studies find no consistent added whitening from the light.
LED whitening kit.note: Studies of light activation have found no consistent whitening beyond the gel alone.
LED whitening kit.overview:
An LED whitening kit combines a peroxide gel, applied by tray, strip or pen, with a small mouthpiece that shines blue or violet LED light on the teeth. It is marketed as a salon-style treatment for home use.

The gel is the active whitening agent. The light accessory is the distinguishing feature, and it is the component with the least research support.
LED whitening kit.mechanism: Peroxide gel bleaches by oxidizing stain molecules. The LED is claimed to speed gel breakdown, but the low-power lights in consumer kits deliver little energy, and studies of light activation in professional bleaching find no consistent extra whitening compared with gel alone.
LED whitening kit.risks: Risks are those of the gel: sensitivity and gum irritation. Umbrella reviews report that light or laser activation does not reliably improve whitening and may increase sensitivity if poorly controlled. A narrow signal exists for violet light combined with carbamide peroxide, but the supporting evidence is limited and was tested in professional settings.

Electric toothbrush.summary: Motorized brush; a large Cochrane review found modest plaque and gingivitis reductions versus manual brushing.
Electric toothbrush.overview:
An electric or powered toothbrush uses a motor to drive the brush head in oscillating-rotating, sonic or other high-frequency motions. Many models add pressure sensors and timers to guide a two-minute brushing routine.

For appearance, the practical gains cited are cleaner teeth, less stain-trapping plaque and healthier gums, which together support a brighter, fresher-looking smile.
Electric toothbrush.mechanism: The motorized head performs thousands of strokes per minute, which removes plaque more consistently than many people manage by hand, and built-in timers and pressure alerts improve technique. Sonic models also create fluid movement around the bristles.
Electric toothbrush.risks: Side effects are rare and minor, mainly gum abrasion if pressed too hard. The large Cochrane review found modest advantages for powered brushes in plaque (about 11 to 21 percent) and gingivitis (about 6 to 11 percent), with the authors noting the clinical importance is uncertain. Manufacturers' premium claims often exceed that evidence, and mid-priced oscillating models are reported to perform similarly.

Water flosser.summary: Pulsed-water oral irrigator for interdental cleaning; reviews report improved gum inflammation, with inconsistent effects on plaque.
Water flosser.overview:
A water flosser, or oral irrigator, shoots a pulsing jet of water between teeth and along the gumline to flush out plaque and food debris. Countertop and cordless handheld versions are sold under brands such as Waterpik.

In appearance terms it is chiefly a gum-health tool, used by people with braces, implants or bridges, or who find string floss hard to use.
Water flosser.mechanism: Pulsed water pressure dislodges loosely attached plaque and bacteria from interdental spaces and shallow pockets, and the massaging action is thought to reduce gingival inflammation and bleeding.
Water flosser.risks: Safety is good; excessive pressure can bruise gums and it is not recommended straight after oral surgery. Systematic reviews show reliable improvements in gingival inflammation but inconsistent effects on plaque, and a recent meta-analysis found no extra benefit over regular floss for general patients. Many supporting trials are industry funded, and water flossers are generally described as an alternative to floss rather than a clear improvement on it.

Tongue scraper.summary: Curved strip drawn over the tongue to remove coating; reviews report small, short-term reductions in breath compounds.
Tongue scraper.overview:
A tongue scraper is a thin curved strip of metal or plastic drawn across the surface of the tongue to remove the whitish coating of bacteria, food debris and dead cells. The practice has long historical roots, including in Ayurvedic tradition.

It is used to reduce bad breath and keep the mouth feeling clean, which users link to social confidence and close-range appearance.
Tongue scraper.mechanism: Most oral malodor comes from sulfur compounds produced by bacteria that colonize the rough tongue dorsum. Scraping physically removes the coating and the bacteria and substrates within it, lowering volatile sulfur compounds for a period.
Tongue scraper.risks: Side effects are minor: gagging, soreness or occasional bleeding if scraped too hard. Cochrane and later reviews found a small short-term reduction in breath compounds compared with toothbrushing, based on very small trials, and insufficient evidence for chronic halitosis. Dental guidance is that breath that stays bad despite cleaning warrants a dental or medical check for gum disease or other causes.

Clear aligners.summary: Removable transparent trays that gradually move teeth; reviews report good results for mild to moderate alignment in suitable cases.
Clear aligners.note: Treatment requires dentist or orthodontist assessment of suitability; mail-order versions omit that step.
Clear aligners.overview:
Clear aligners are a series of removable, transparent plastic trays, each shaped slightly differently, that gradually move teeth toward a planned position. Brands include Invisalign and a range of dentist-supervised and direct-to-consumer systems.

They are used to straighten crooked or crowded teeth, close gaps and correct some bite problems, with the added appeal of being nearly invisible compared with metal braces.
Clear aligners.mechanism: Each tray is thermoformed from a digital treatment plan and applies light, controlled force that remodels the bone around the tooth root. Bonded composite attachments give the plastic grip to produce movements like rotation, and trays are typically changed every one to two weeks.
Clear aligners.risks: Reviews show aligners work well for mild to moderate alignment, leveling and some intrusion, but are less predictable for rotations, extrusion and root control, especially in extraction cases. Risks include gum recession, root resorption, relapse without retainers, and poor outcomes when worn too little. A dentist or orthodontist confirms suitability, and mail-order and DIY versions omit that safeguard.

Bruxism night guard.summary: Plastic appliance worn during sleep to protect teeth from grinding; reviews find little direct evidence it reduces wear or cures bruxism.
Bruxism night guard.overview:
A bruxism night guard, or occlusal splint, is a hard or soft plastic appliance worn over the teeth during sleep to protect them from grinding and clenching. Custom guards are made by a dentist, while stock and boil-and-bite versions are sold over the counter.

It is used to prevent enamel wear, chipping and flattening of teeth, which over years can change how the smile looks.
Bruxism night guard.mechanism: The guard places a plastic barrier between the upper and lower teeth so grinding forces wear the appliance instead of the enamel. It does not stop the underlying muscle activity, which is linked to stress, sleep arousals and other factors.
Bruxism night guard.risks: Splints are widely used and generally safe, but reviews find little direct evidence that they reduce tooth wear, and insufficient evidence that they cure bruxism itself; some designs may increase clenching or cause bite changes with full-time use. Ill-fitting or hard stock guards can be uncomfortable. Dental guidance is that a dentist assess for sleep apnea and other drivers.

Jaw exerciser.summary: Resistance device for the chewing muscles; no controlled trial shows it improves jawline definition, and larger masseters broaden the lower face.
Jaw exerciser.note: Overuse is reported to strain the temporomandibular joint (TMJ).
Jaw exerciser.overview:
A jaw exerciser is a silicone or plastic device, often a ball or resistance trainer, that the user bites or chews against to work the masseter and related chewing muscles. It is promoted on social media for a sharper, more defined jawline.

The devices sit in the looksmaxxing space alongside hard gum and chewing routines, where bigger jaw muscles are assumed to produce better jaw definition.
Jaw exerciser.mechanism: Resistance chewing loads the masseter and temporalis, which can increase muscle stiffness, endurance and in some cases size. Muscle growth widens the lower face at the angle of the jaw rather than removing fat or changing bone structure.
Jaw exerciser.risks: No controlled trial has shown that the devices improve jawline definition; the available literature consists of small studies on muscle stiffness and a two-person case report finding no change in the jawline or double chin. Overuse can strain the temporomandibular joint and cause jaw pain, headaches and tooth wear. People with TMJ symptoms are generally advised to avoid them.

Mastic / hard gum.summary: Resin-based hard chewing gum used to work the masseter; its effect on jawline definition has not been shown in controlled studies.
Mastic / hard gum.overview:
Mastic gum is a hard, chewy resin from the mastic tree (Pistacia lentiscus) grown mainly on the Greek island of Chios, and it is marketed alongside harder-than-normal gums such as Turkish falim as a jaw-training gum. Several brands now sell mastic-based jawline gum.

It is used in looksmaxxing circles as a food-based way to work the masseter and encourage a more defined lower face.
Mastic / hard gum.mechanism: Prolonged hard chewing makes the masseter and temporalis work against resistance, which may raise muscle stiffness, endurance and possibly size over time. The resin itself has traditional digestive uses, but any jaw effect is attributed to the chewing load, not the substance.
Mastic / hard gum.risks: No controlled study shows mastic gum sculpts the jawline; small studies cover muscle stiffness and oxygen dynamics, not definition. Heavy chewing is associated with jaw muscle pain, TMJ strain and uneven wear, and larger masseters broaden rather than sharpen the face. Forum users themselves raise TMJ concerns, and the jawline effect is unproven.

Mouth tape.summary: Tape over the lips at night to encourage nasal breathing; reviews find only small preliminary studies, and jaw-remodeling claims lack evidence.
Mouth tape.note: Reviewers caution about use with undiagnosed sleep apnea or nasal obstruction.
Mouth tape.overview:
Mouth taping means placing a strip of gentle tape over the lips at night to keep the mouth closed and encourage nasal breathing. It spread through social media with claims of better sleep, less snoring, fresher breath and a better jawline.

In looksmaxxing circles it is tied to the idea that nasal breathing shapes adult facial structure, a claim for which no supporting evidence has been published.
Mouth tape.mechanism: Sealing the lips forces air through the nose, which filters and humidifies it and may reduce dry mouth. Any effect on jaw shape has not been established, because adult facial bone does not meaningfully remodel with breathing route.
Mouth tape.risks: Systematic and scoping reviews find only small, preliminary studies, with one small trial in mouth-breathers with mild sleep apnea suggesting possible benefit, and conclude that demonstrated benefit is minimal. The main concerns are taping over nasal obstruction or undiagnosed sleep apnea, skin irritation and suffocation anxiety. Clinicians advise that people with snoring, daytime sleepiness or blocked nasal airways be evaluated before trying it.

Mewing appliances.summary: Palate-expanding or tongue-posture devices sold alongside mewing; no controlled evidence shows adult skeletal change from them.
Mewing appliances.overview:
Mewing appliances are palate-expanding or tongue-posture devices, including mouthpieces and plates, sold to supplement the practice of mewing, in which the tongue is held against the roof of the mouth in the hope of remodeling the jaw and midface. The practice comes from orthotropics, developed by John Mew.

It is a central idea in looksmaxxing forums, where users seek a more forward jaw, higher cheekbones and a sharper jawline.
Mewing appliances.mechanism: The theory is that sustained tongue pressure on the palate changes how facial bones grow. This is considered plausible in growing children with proper orthodontic appliances, but no controlled evidence of skeletal change in adults from tongue posture or over-the-counter appliances has been published.
Mewing appliances.risks: No randomized trials or controlled studies of mewing in adults were found; orthodontic bodies say there is no reliable evidence it reshapes the jaw. Forcing a tongue posture or wearing ill-fitting appliances can strain the jaw joint, shift teeth or cause discomfort. Myofunctional therapy supervised by a clinician has modest support for specific conditions such as sleep-disordered breathing, which is a different claim. The scholarly links listed are the closest relevant research identified, not studies of mewing itself.

Red light LED mask.summary: Wearable red and near-infrared light panel (photobiomodulation); sham-controlled trials report modest improvements in fine lines and elasticity.
Red light LED mask.overview:
A red light LED mask is a wearable panel that emits red and often near-infrared light, typically around 630 to 850 nanometers, against the face for several minutes at a time. It is a home version of low-level light therapy used in dermatology clinics.

It is marketed for fine lines, skin tone and texture, and post-procedure recovery, and is one of the better-studied home beauty device categories.
Red light LED mask.mechanism: Red and near-infrared light is absorbed by mitochondrial enzymes such as cytochrome c oxidase in skin cells, which is thought to boost cellular energy and stimulate fibroblasts to make collagen while reducing inflammation. This process is called photobiomodulation.
Red light LED mask.risks: Eye exposure is the main safety concern, so goggles or closed eyes are advised, and mild warmth or redness is possible. Sham-controlled trials show modest improvements in crow's feet and skin elasticity, but studies are small, often short and sometimes industry sponsored, and devices vary widely in dose and wavelength. Effects fade if treatment stops, and reported results are subtle.

Blue light acne device.summary: Handheld or mask device emitting blue light; meta-analyses report some reduction in inflammatory acne lesions from small, short trials.
Blue light acne device.overview:
A blue light acne device is a handheld wand or mask that emits visible blue light, around 405 to 470 nanometers, onto acne-prone skin for a few minutes a day. Dermatology clinics use stronger versions, and consumer devices are lower power.

It is used as a drug-free adjunct for mild to moderate inflammatory acne.
Blue light acne device.mechanism: Cutibacterium acnes produces porphyrins that absorb blue light and generate reactive oxygen species, damaging the bacteria. The light may also have a mild anti-inflammatory effect on the skin.
Blue light acne device.risks: Side effects are minor, such as temporary dryness or redness, and eye protection is advised. Meta-analyses find blue light can reduce lesions, but included trials are small, short and at risk of bias, so effectiveness versus standard treatments remains unclear. Combination blue and red light may do better in the short term, and home devices are weaker than clinic units.

At-home fractional laser.summary: Low-energy handheld fractional laser for fine lines and texture; a 2026 device review ranked the category among the stronger home devices, varying by device.
At-home fractional laser.overview:
At-home fractional lasers are low-energy, non-ablative handheld devices that treat the skin in a grid of tiny microscopic zones rather than the whole surface. They are sold for fine lines, uneven texture and mild scarring on the face.

They are a consumer version of professional fractional resurfacing and are positioned as one of the stronger device categories for home use, though far gentler than clinic treatments.
At-home fractional laser.mechanism: The laser creates microscopic thermal injury columns in the epidermis and dermis, surrounded by untouched skin, which triggers wound healing and new collagen production. Home devices deliver much lower energy, so changes accumulate gradually over repeated sessions.
At-home fractional laser.risks: Possible effects include redness, dryness, temporary pigment change and, with misuse, burns or infection; sun protection and skin-type suitability matter. Reviews of home devices rank fractional lasers, LED and radiofrequency as having the best efficacy-safety balance, but no systematic review focused only on home fractional lasers was found and quality of evidence varies by device. Results are modest compared with clinic procedures.

RF skin-tightening device.summary: Low-power radiofrequency device that warms the dermis; small trials report modest wrinkle improvement with continued use.
RF skin-tightening device.overview:
A home radiofrequency skin-tightening device uses low-power radio waves delivered through metal electrodes pressed against the face to warm the skin. It is sold for wrinkles, lax skin and a firmer facial contour.

It is a lower-power relative of clinic radiofrequency treatments and is one of the home devices with published randomized data.
RF skin-tightening device.mechanism: Radiofrequency energy heats the dermis, which shrinks existing collagen fibers and prompts fibroblasts to produce new collagen over weeks. Consistent use is needed because each session delivers only mild heating.
RF skin-tightening device.risks: Reported effects are mild redness and warmth, with burns possible from overheating or poor contact. Small randomized and open-label trials show modest wrinkle improvement, but wrinkle scores decline again after use stops, and many studies are short and sponsor-linked. Reported results are subtle tightening rather than the effect of a surgical facelift.

Microcurrent device.summary: Passes very low electrical current into the face; users report an immediate lifted look, and evidence for lasting effect is thin.
Microcurrent device.overview:
Microcurrent devices pass very low electrical current, in the microampere range, into the face through metal or gel-coated probes. They are sold as a non-invasive facelift that tones the muscles and lifts the contour.

An instantly tighter look is commonly reported, and the devices are popular as a pre-event routine.
Microcurrent device.mechanism: The current is claimed to mimic the body's own electrical signals, stimulating facial muscles and cellular energy production. The visible lifting is thought to come from temporary muscle activation and fluid shifts rather than structural change in skin.
Microcurrent device.risks: The devices are generally well tolerated, with tingling or mild redness; they are not suitable for people with pacemakers or certain implants or during pregnancy. Evidence is limited: a review notes few studies specific to home microcurrent devices, and the only randomized trial found was of a neuromuscular stimulation device. Effects are short-lived without continued use.

Multi-head facial tool.summary: All-in-one handsets such as TheraFace combining LED, microcurrent and massage heads; the LED head has trial data, while other heads have little independent evidence.
Multi-head facial tool.overview:
Multi-head facial tools, of which TheraFace-type devices are an example, combine interchangeable attachments in one handset, typically LED light, microcurrent, percussive massage, cleansing and cold or heat heads.

They are sold as an all-in-one skincare routine and appeal to users who want several modalities without separate gadgets.
Multi-head facial tool.mechanism: Each head works by a different mechanism: LED photobiomodulation for collagen and inflammation, microcurrent for muscle stimulation, percussion and temperature for circulation and puffiness. The benefit depends on which heads have supporting evidence.
Multi-head facial tool.risks: Light-based heads have randomized, sham-controlled data for wrinkle and elasticity gains, but the microcurrent and massage heads have little independent evidence, and most multi-function devices are tested as a package or alongside serums. Costs are high and reported results modest. The same cautions apply as for each mode, including eye and pacemaker precautions.

Sonic cleansing brush.summary: Oscillating-bristle cleansing device; small studies report better particulate and makeup removal than hand washing, with few randomized trials.
Sonic cleansing brush.overview:
A sonic cleansing brush is a handheld device with a soft bristle head that oscillates at high frequency while cleansing the face. Clarisonic popularized the category, and many brands now sell similar tools.

It is used for deeper removal of makeup, oil and pollution than hands alone and for a smoother-feeling surface.
Sonic cleansing brush.mechanism: The head vibrates thousands of times per minute, loosening debris and sebum from pores and the skin surface, which makes cleansers work more effectively than manual washing.
Sonic cleansing brush.risks: Overuse or rough settings can irritate or over-exfoliate skin, especially for sensitive or acne-prone skin, and bristle heads need replacing to avoid bacterial build-up. Evidence is modest: a clinician review and small studies show better particulate removal and acne improvement in uncontrolled cohorts, but few randomized trials. The documented effect is cleansing rather than anti-aging.

Dermaplaning razor.summary: Single-blade facial razor that removes dead skin and fine facial hair; effects last only a few weeks.
Dermaplaning razor.overview:
Dermaplaning is a form of mechanical exfoliation in which a single sharp blade is drawn lightly across the face to remove the top layer of dead skin cells and fine vellus hair, or peach fuzz. Home versions use small, single-blade facial razors, while professionals use a scalpel.

It is used to get a smoother skin surface, brighter look and more even makeup and skincare application.
Dermaplaning razor.mechanism: The blade, held at a shallow angle, shaves off the stratum corneum and vellus hair at skin level. The hair follicle is untouched, so hair regrows on its normal schedule, and exfoliation lets products absorb more easily.
Dermaplaning razor.risks: Risks include nicks, irritation and breakouts, and it is not advised over active acne or inflamed skin. Hair does not grow back thicker or darker, but the effects last only a few weeks. No controlled trials were identified, and the evidence comes from clinic and aesthetics sources, though the mechanism is physically straightforward. Using a clean blade is advised to reduce infection risk.

Derma roller (home).summary: Handheld needle roller (0.25 to 0.5 mm) for scars and texture; collagen evidence is for professional microneedling, and home use carries infection risk.
Derma roller (home).note: The 2026 device review singled out home microneedling for limited evidence and risk.
Derma roller (home).overview:
A home derma roller is a handheld roller covered in tiny needles, usually 0.25 to 0.5 millimeters at home, rolled across the skin to create microscopic punctures. It is a consumer version of professional microneedling.

It is promoted for scars, texture, fine lines and better absorption of serums.
Derma roller (home).mechanism: Needle punctures trigger a wound-healing response that increases collagen and elastin production in the dermis. Professional devices use longer needles to reach deeper layers, while shorter home needles are reported to produce less effect.
Derma roller (home).risks: Home use carries a risk of infection, irritation, post-inflammatory pigmentation and scarring if the roller is not sterilized or technique is poor. Reviews note that proper sterilization is essential for home rollers. The collagen evidence is for professional microneedling, not home rolling, and no systematic review of home rollers specifically was found.

Gua sha stone.summary: Smooth-edged tool used in facial massage; moves fluid temporarily, with no evidence of lasting structural change.
Gua sha stone.overview:
Gua sha is a traditional East Asian technique in which a smooth-edged tool, often of jade or rose quartz, is drawn over lubricated skin. A gentler facial version is used in skincare for sculpting and de-puffing.

It is popular on social media as a lymphatic massage and facial contouring step.
Gua sha stone.mechanism: The pressure and stroking motion transiently increase local blood flow and move fluid, which can reduce puffiness for a time. No evidence of lasting structural changes to fat or bone has been reported.
Gua sha stone.risks: Facial use is low risk, though pressing too hard can bruise, and traditional body scraping intentionally raises red marks. The evidence concerns pain relief in the body, which is of low quality, and cosmetic claims for the face have not been substantiated. Results are temporary.

Ice roller.summary: Chilled roller used briefly on the face; cold causes short-term vasoconstriction that reduces puffiness.
Ice roller.overview:
An ice roller is a handheld roller with a chilled head, either a frozen gel or a metal cylinder, that is rolled over the face. It is used in short sessions to reduce morning puffiness and calm skin.

It is mainly used the morning of an event for a fresher, less swollen look.
Ice roller.mechanism: Cold causes local vasoconstriction, reducing blood flow and fluid leakage into tissue, which lessens puffiness and redness for a short time. The effect fades as the skin rewarms.
Ice roller.risks: Risks are minimal if skin is not frozen for long; direct prolonged contact is advised against, and people with cold urticaria, Raynaud's or sensitivity to cold should be cautious. No trial of cold rollers on everyday facial puffiness was identified; the closest evidence is on cold-induced vasoconstriction and post-surgical swelling, so the benefit is considered plausible but short-lived.

Pimple patches.summary: Hydrocolloid stickers placed over blemishes to absorb drainage and block picking; acne-specific evidence is thin.
Pimple patches.overview:
Pimple patches are small adhesive stickers, usually hydrocolloid, placed over a blemish for several hours or overnight. Some also contain salicylic acid or microneedles.

They are used to flatten whiteheads and protect spots from picking.
Pimple patches.mechanism: The hydrocolloid layer absorbs fluid and pus from the lesion and holds a moist, protected environment that supports healing. The patch also acts as a physical barrier that discourages touching and bacterial contamination.
Pimple patches.risks: Side effects are rare, mainly adhesive irritation or allergy, and they are not effective for deep cystic acne. Evidence is limited: a narrative review says hydrocolloids are studied mostly for wounds with few acne studies, and the one randomized trial found compared two patches rather than with no treatment. They are described as a plausible low-risk aid for individual spots rather than a treatment for acne.

Silicone scar sheets.summary: Medical-grade silicone sheets worn over healed scars; Cochrane reviews rate the evidence low certainty, with some trials showing improved thickness and color.
Silicone scar sheets.overview:
Silicone scar sheets are adhesive, reusable sheets of medical-grade silicone applied over a healed scar for most of the day for weeks to months. They are used for raised hypertrophic scars and keloids, and are sometimes applied after surgery or acne.

They are a standard first-line, non-invasive option and an inexpensive way to treat a visible scar.
Silicone scar sheets.mechanism: Silicone hydrates the outer skin layer and is thought to regulate fibroblast activity and collagen production through occlusion and gentle pressure, softening and flattening the scar.
Silicone scar sheets.risks: Side effects are rash, itching or maceration, and sheets must be kept clean. Cochrane reviews describe the evidence as limited and low to very low certainty, with trials of poor quality, though some show improved thickness and color. Reported benefits are modest, and consistent wear is required.

Under-eye cooling mask.summary: Reusable gel or cold patch worn over the lower eyelids; cooling temporarily reduces swelling, with evidence drawn from post-surgery studies.
Under-eye cooling mask.overview:
An under-eye cooling mask is a reusable gel or cold-pack patch worn over the lower eyelids and cheeks for a few minutes. It is used to reduce puffy eyes after sleep or a late night.

It is a quick, low-cost morning routine for a more rested look.
Under-eye cooling mask.mechanism: Cooling causes vasoconstriction and reduces fluid accumulation in the loose periorbital tissue, easing swelling and redness temporarily.
Under-eye cooling mask.risks: Risks are very low, with rare cold urticaria or skin irritation. Evidence comes from post-surgery swelling studies, where cold gel masks outperformed ice gloves, and not from everyday puffiness, so benefits are considered plausible and short-lived. Persistent bags or swelling can reflect fat, allergy or medical causes that cooling does not address.

High-frequency wand.summary: Glass-electrode device producing a violet glow, marketed for acne and pores; the only study found was in vitro, and no human trials were located.
High-frequency wand.overview:
A high-frequency wand is a handheld glass electrode that produces a low-current, high-voltage alternating current, giving a violet glow and ozone smell. It descends from the old Darsonval devices and is marketed for acne, pores and anti-aging.

It appears in skincare routines as a spot treatment, but the claims are largely unproven.
High-frequency wand.mechanism: The current is said to generate ozone and mild heat that kill acne bacteria and boost circulation. Only laboratory evidence supports an antibacterial effect.
High-frequency wand.risks: Risks include irritation and burns from misuse, and it is contraindicated with pacemakers or pregnancy. The only study found tested a similar device in vitro against skin bacteria, with no human trials located, so the claims are unproven. It has not been shown to substitute for established acne treatment.

Face slimming strap.summary: Elastic chin-and-head band marketed for double chin and jawline definition; no clinical study of compression straps was found.
Face slimming strap.overview:
A face slimming strap is an elastic band worn under the chin and over the head to compress the lower face and neck. It is marketed for reducing a double chin and defining the jawline.

It is mostly sold through social media and online marketplaces.
Face slimming strap.mechanism: The strap presses on the skin and underlying tissue, which may briefly push fluid away or hold the jaw in position. It does not remove fat cells or change bone.
Face slimming strap.risks: Risks are skin irritation, discomfort and unmet expectations, and tight wear could affect breathing or sleep. No clinical study of compression straps was found; reviews of submental fullness support injections, cryolipolysis and energy devices instead, while a jaw-exercise case report found no change. The closest evidence does not support the marketing claims.

Nose reshaping clip.summary: Soft clip marketed to lift the nasal tip or narrow the bridge; adult cartilage and bone are rigid, with no controlled trials.
Nose reshaping clip.overview:
A nose reshaping clip is a soft plastic or silicone device that pinches the nose, often worn for hours, and is marketed as a way to lift the tip or narrow the bridge without surgery. Similar items are called nose shapers or lifters.

It appeals to people seeking rhinoplasty-like results at lower cost.
Nose reshaping clip.mechanism: The clip applies external pressure to the cartilage and soft tissue. In infants, nasal molding can reshape soft cartilage, but adult cartilage and bone are rigid and do not change with sustained pressure.
Nose reshaping clip.risks: Risks are skin irritation, pressure marks and breathing discomfort. No controlled trials of splints or clips for adult nasal shaping were found; the nearest evidence concerns nasal molding in infants and non-surgical filler rhinoplasty, which are different interventions. The claim is unsupported by published evidence, and cosmetic changes to the nose are normally assessed by a surgeon.

Facial lifting tape.summary: Adhesive strips that pull skin back to smooth it temporarily; the lift lasts only while the tape is worn.
Facial lifting tape.overview:
Facial lifting tape consists of adhesive strips or invisible patches placed on the cheeks, jawline or temples and pulled back, often hidden by hair, to temporarily smooth and lift sagging skin. It has been used in photography, TV and event styling for years.

The effect is cosmetic and immediate, and lasts only while the tape is on.
Facial lifting tape.mechanism: The adhesive physically holds skin in a tighter position, so the lift is mechanical, not biological. No change in collagen or tissue structure occurs.
Facial lifting tape.risks: Risks are skin irritation, adhesive allergy and redness on removal, and wearing it overnight can leave marks. Studies on facial tape concern post-surgical swelling and the mechanics of taped skin, not anti-aging, so the research does not support long-term claims. The effect is reliable but temporary.

Lip plumping device.summary: Suction cup that draws blood and fluid into the lips for a few hours of swelling; no peer-reviewed study of suction devices was found.
Lip plumping device.overview:
A lip plumping device is a small cup or suction tool placed over the lips to draw blood and fluid into the tissue, producing a temporary swelling. Some versions add vibration or heat.

It is a do-it-yourself alternative to lip filler for a fuller look for a few hours.
Lip plumping device.mechanism: Negative pressure pulls blood into the lip tissue and causes mild swelling and engorgement. No new tissue is created, so the effect fades quickly.
Lip plumping device.risks: Too much suction can cause bruising, broken capillaries, pain or swelling, and results are short-lived. No peer-reviewed study of suction lip devices was found, only patents. The scholarly source listed concerns hyaluronic acid filler, which is a different intervention, and is included as the nearest research on lip enhancement safety.

Facial exerciser.summary: Silicone or resistance devices for cheek and smile muscles; evidence for aesthetic outcomes is weak, and no trial tested the devices themselves.
Facial exerciser.overview:
Facial exercisers are small silicone or resistance devices placed in the mouth or on the cheeks to work the smile and cheek muscles, and are promoted alongside facial yoga routines. They are marketed for fuller cheeks, less sagging and a more youthful face.

The idea is to tone facial muscles the way gym training builds body muscle.
Facial exerciser.mechanism: Repeated contraction against resistance may enlarge or strengthen the facial muscles, increasing cheek volume in the area they cover. Whether this meaningfully changes how the face looks is less clear.
Facial exerciser.risks: Overuse can cause muscle soreness, jaw tension or temporomandibular strain, and repeated expressions may deepen some lines. Evidence is limited: the main study was a small uncontrolled trial of facial exercise in middle-aged women with high dropout and a conflict of interest, showing modest cheek fullness improvement. No trial tested the devices themselves.
